nodes.label: FRIC Website Content, Design & Technical Specification v1.0 (client brief, prepared by FRIC, status: Approved for Design Execution) — the single execution reference for the appointed design/development partner
nodes.author: FRIC

nodes.label: Define the Undefined — FRIC's core brand philosophy/proposition (§07); reused throughout the proposal as its central framing device

FRIC brand architecture (§07): philosophy = Define the Undefined; promise = Help You Stand Out; motto = We Dare. We Can.; business expression = What We Build; operating expression = Define-Engineer-Validate-Deliver
Define - Engineer - Validate - Deliver — FRIC's operating-model expression, used as the fixed 'How We Build' section on every capability page, deliberately without proprietary detail

Document control (§02): spec v1.0, status Approved for Design Execution, owner FRIC; agency may recommend refinements but must not redefine FRIC's business narrative without written approval; all metrics/claims/certifications must be FRIC-verified before publication

Executive summary (§03): website must make FRIC understandable to a senior visitor, credible to a buying committee, discoverable via search+AI — six pillars: Brand, Business clarity, Differentiation, Trust, Conversion, Scalability

Project overview & scope (§04): reposition FRIC from product/POSM vendor to global commercial-operations partner; improve lead quality not just traffic; in-scope IA/UX/design-system/CMS/SEO-GEO; out-of-scope final translation/data migration/proprietary software/customer-supplier portals

Target audience strategy (§05): buying centre similar to HH Global/GEP/Ogilvy/Tag — CEO/COO, CPO/Procurement Director, CMO/Marketing Director, Marketing Procurement/Category Lead, Marketing Ops/Brand Lead, Supply Chain Director, Sourcing Manager/Buyer, Finance/Legal/Compliance

Buying centre, decision criteria & entry intent (§06): five buying roles — Discoverer, Technical evaluator, Business influencer, Approver, Operational user — each with distinct needs/next actions; six decision criteria
Benchmark — McKinsey (§08): adopt narrative journeys, every-page entry, in-page anchors, content ecosystem, subscribe actions; do not copy dense consultancy vocabulary
Benchmark — Accenture (§08): adopt trend-led storytelling, strong transitions, capability+insight relationships, bold hero logic; avoid tech theatre / generic 'reinvention' language
Benchmark — Deloitte (§08): adopt clear service/industry structures, executive language, disciplined hierarchy; avoid high content density and institutional complexity
Benchmark — HH Global / Tag / Ogilvy (§08): adopt recognizable marketing-procurement/production/activation language and case-led proof; avoid capability lists without upstream problem framing
Benchmark — GEP (§08): adopt procurement taxonomy, research resources, software/service clarity; avoid platform-first positioning or procurement-technology jargon
Benchmark — Apple / Stripe (§08): adopt whitespace, typography, component discipline, restrained motion; avoid consumer-product aesthetics that weaken B2B credibility

Website philosophy — every page is an entry page (§09): homepage is a brand hub not a mandatory first step; visitors may land via Google/AI search/LinkedIn/referral/RFP/internal sharing; each major page must independently establish context, relevance, evidence and next action
Primary website architecture (§10): nav = Home | Who We Are | What We Build | Industries | Insights | Contact; careers/policies/accessibility/locations/partners live in footer

Content ecosystem — connected knowledge system (§11): 8 content types (Capability, Industry, Commercial Observation, Article/Research, White Paper, Framework, Case Study, Who We Are) each with required, bidirectional related-content links in the CMS

Content layer architecture (§12): full internal logic (Business Drivers→Reality→Evidence→Impact→Need→What We Build→How We Build→Proof→Conversion) compressed into a simpler visitor-facing flow (Hero→Why It Matters→What We Build→How We Build→Proof→Contact/Subscribe)

Website narrative architecture (§13): six-stage flow — Business Drivers→Business Reality→Business Impact→Business Need→What We Build→Proof & Conversion; section transitions must answer 'why continue?' and are written into copy, not separate blocks

Business drivers (§14): regulation evolution, creativity/format diversification, workforce experience fragmentation, transaction complexity, personalized end-market demand, AI accelerates processing not definition

Business reality (§15): eight recurring operating realities e.g. requirements harder to define/maintain, knowledge dispersed, expert guidance not continuously available, solutions/quotations become incomparable, global consistency harder to maintain

Business impact & causal chain (§16): incomplete input→different interpretations→incomparable options→rework/delay→cost transfer→commercial loss (project deviation, rush cost, launch delay, lost sales, employee burnout)

Mode boundary matrix — existing-approach capability boundaries (§17): integrated procurement, large supplier networks, AI/digital tools and experienced teams each do some things well but cannot guarantee requirement accuracy or solution suitability — rationale: the website must show these become most effective once the project itself is properly defined, not argue they are ineffective

Commercial evidence — Commercial Observations (§18): FRIC's signature concise, citeable, experience-based truths, e.g. 'A quotation request is not a project definition' and 'A product image is not a manufacturing specification'

Business need (§19): organizations need expert-level commercial guidance & enterprise knowledge throughout the project — enterprise knowledge, progressive definition, capability engineering, integrated operations, AI-enabled acceleration, commercial accountability; public pages must not expose proprietary knowledge structures
Capability — Marketing Procurement (§20): build execution-ready marketing-procurement operations around accurate requirements, category knowledge, accountable delivery
Capability — Global POSM (§20): build scalable, compliant, locally-adaptable POSM and retail-display operations
Capability — Global Supply Chain (§20): build resilient global supply chains across sourcing, trade, compliance, logistics, local support
Capability — Strategic Sourcing (§20): build sourcing strategies on category intelligence, capability fit, total cost, risk
Capability — Commercial Delivery (§20): build dependable project delivery from commercial direction to market-ready result
Capability — Requirement Engineering (§20): turn business objectives, images and briefs into clear commercial/technical requirements
Capability — Capability Engineering (§20): identify, validate and combine the capabilities required to deliver the right solution
Page template — Home (§21): Hero(Define the Undefined)→Commercial Reality(3-6 drivers)→What We Build→How We Build→Proof→Featured Insights→Final conversion→Footer; one dominant message per screen
Page template — Who We Are (§22): Hero→Why We Exist→Our Philosophy→Operating Model→Experience→Values→Global Capability→CTA; must not become a customer pain-point page
Page template — Capability (§23): fixed required order Hero→Why It Matters→What We Build→How We Build→Proof→Related→Contact; each capability page is a complete standalone landing page

Sample content structure — Marketing Procurement worked example (§24): H1/proposition/reality/impact/need, 'What FRIC builds' list, suggested observation 'A quotation request is not a project definition', primary CTA 'Discuss Your Marketing Procurement Requirement'
Industry — FMCG (§25 launch industry)
Industry — Food & Beverage (§25 launch industry)
Industry — Healthcare (§25 launch industry)
Industry — Optical (§25 launch industry)

Page template — Industry (§25): Hero→Industry reality(4-6 drivers)→Relevant capabilities(subset)→Industry observations→Proof→Related insights→Contact; launch FMCG/Food&Beverage/Healthcare/Optical, expandable to Luxury/Retail/Consumer Electronics

Page template — Insights (§26): five content families (Commercial Observation, Article/Research, Framework, White Paper, News) each with required structure; index filterable by type/topic/industry/date; must not operate as a news archive

Page template — Proof assets (§27): Case Study (outcome→context→challenge→why-prior-approach-insufficient→FRIC solution→verified result→lessons→related) and White Paper (executive summary→drivers→analysis→framework→recommendations→download); case claims require client approval or anonymization; white papers need an indexable public summary even when the PDF is gated

Customer entry journeys / user journey (§28): design for multiple entry points (Search/AI answer, LinkedIn/Email, Referral/RFP, Homepage) and commitment levels; primary conversion = Discuss Your Project contact form with contextual prefill; secondary = subscribe/download/view/watch

Action transitions & CTA architecture (§29): every major section must create a reason to continue, with one dominant action per section — no equal-weight button stacks; transition-logic table Hero→Why It Matters→What We Build→How We Build→Proof→Insight→Case
Desktop experience (§30): fuller commercial narrative, optional on-page anchor nav, wide editorial layouts/comparison blocks, one major proposition per screen, 3-6 items per structured block

Mobile experience (§31): distinct information-priority design, not a scaled-down desktop page; preserve content parity for search; convert matrices to stacked comparison cards; test real EN/ZH content before approval; mobile-first indexing requires content-parity (technical ref T5)

Visual direction & brand system (§32): white/warm-neutral space, black type, restrained brand-green accent only, white 'light portal' metaphor (ambiguity→clarity), premium modern grotesk typography (Inter/Inter Display) + editorial serif sparingly, real commercial-environment photography, no factory clichés/handshake stock/unverifiable scale claims

UI/UX system & interaction principles (§33): reusable component system — global header, hero modules, content cards, evidence/comparison/CTA modules, forms, footer; full state set (hover/focus/active/loading/error/success/empty/disabled); accessibility and multilingual content flexibility built in

Functional & CMS requirements (§34): CMS content types, editorial workflow (draft/review/approval/scheduled-publish/archive/preview/roles), content relationships, search/filters, one simple contact form with auto-captured source, subscription, gated downloads with public landing pages, compliance surfaces, integrations, admin (redirect manager/metadata/sitemaps/backups); agency must document CMS/hosting/licensing/costs/ownership/lock-in risk

Multilingual & localization architecture (§35): dedicated URL per locale (no cookies/client-side swap), visible language switcher, no forced IP redirect, per-locale translation/approval status, self-referencing canonical + reciprocal hreflang + x-default, language-specific sitemaps, no uncontrolled machine translation as final copy, no silently-mixed-language fallback

SEO & Google indexing framework (§36): crawlable server-rendered/SSG HTML, one entity+H1 per page, editable metadata, short lowercase-hyphenated URLs, required-field internal linking, automatic XML sitemaps by type/language, JSON-LD structured-data suite (Organization/WebSite/WebPage/BreadcrumbList/Article/Person/VideoObject/Service), 301 redirect map, robots/noindex control, Search Console verification

GEO / AI-search readiness (§37): explicit topic + direct-answer summary near top of every page, stable definitions/named frameworks/dated research/authors/sources, self-contained citeable Commercial Observations, separate fact/inference/opinion/result, semantic HTML not text-in-images, consistent entity naming, allow OAI-SearchBot, govern GPTBot independently for training opt-in/out, track ChatGPT/AI referrals, do not rely on experimental 'GEO score' files

Performance, accessibility, security & analytics (§38): CWV field targets (LCP≤2.5s/INP≤200ms/CLS≤0.1 p75), Lighthouse mobile targets 'to be agreed', WCAG 2.2 AA, responsive AVIF/WebP media, minimal JS/code-splitting, HTTPS/secure headers/backups, GA4+Search Console consent-aware analytics, conversion+journey event tracking, launch dashboard & event dictionary for FRIC's marketing team

Deliverables, acceptance criteria & implementation sequence (§39): full deliverable list (sitemap/wireframes/design system/UI/prototype/component library/CMS/SEO-GEO/analytics/source files+training); nine acceptance criteria incl. senior-visitor relevance without a catalogue, standalone entry pages, distinctive Commercial Observation format, FRIC can publish without agency redesign; six-phase implementation table

Technical references & final agency checklist (§40): T1-T11 official standards (Google Search Central, hreflang/multi-regional/sitemaps/canonical/mobile-first docs, OpenAI crawler docs, web.dev Core Web Vitals, W3C WCAG 2.2, Schema.org); agency confirmation checklists before design approval and before launch
Google Search Central SEO documentation (T1-T6) — developers.google.com/search/docs, hreflang, multi-regional sites, sitemaps, canonical URLs, mobile-first indexing
OpenAI crawler & publisher documentation (T7-T8) — OpenAI Crawlers overview + Publishers and Developers FAQ
web.dev Core Web Vitals (T9) + W3C WCAG 2.2 (T10) — external performance and accessibility standards
Schema.org current vocabulary (T11) — schema.org/version/latest
